adjudicator_reports.spec_defects:
Places the spec is silent, ambiguous, or self-contradictory (none of these changed an answer above, but each is a latent hole):

1. 1.2 defines counting only forward ("a period of n days from date D begins on D+1"), yet 2.3 requires a backward measurement ("registration date fewer than 30 days before the checkout date"). 1.2 says it is "measured the same way" without saying which endpoint is D. T05 (27 days) is safe on any reading, but a case at 29/30/31 days would be undecidable.

2. 4.3 re-shelving is doubly loose. (a) "the item is shelved the following day" — following the end of the extended period, or the day after the natural 4-day period? (b) "with a fresh 4-day period counted from that day" does not re-cite 1.2, so whether the shelving day is counted is left to inference. T17 turns on both; importing 1.2's global convention yields 22 March, but readings producing 21 or 23 March are only weakly excluded.

3. 4.3 adjusts only the LAST day of a collection period for closure. It says nothing about a shelving day (or a re-shelving day) that falls on a closed day, even though 1.4 lets returns happen on closed days and 1.6 bars in-person collection on closed days — so a period can begin on a day the member cannot act.

4. 5.1 states a loan "carries at most one invocation" but never states the consequence of a second attempt: is the second invocation void (leaving the request judged on ordinary rules), or does it invalidate the request outright? T30 reaches DENIED either way, but a fact pattern with no other bar would be undecidable.

5. 6.3 fixes suspension by balance "at that moment", while 7.2's deemed order is a rule about events, not about balances. The spec never expressly says the deemed order also fixes the balance at the moment of a later same-date event. T15 depends on that inference.

6. 7.2's deemed order omits several event types that the rules make operative: fee postings and forfeit charges under 6.5/6.4, and the act of shelving under 4.3. A same-date return-plus-hold-placement (not tested here) would leave it unsettled whether the hold is in the queue when the item is shelved.

7. 3.2 defines the window as "the effective due date and the two dates immediately before it" without saying whether those two dates skip closed days. Since renewals may be made on closed days (1.6), calendar dates is the natural reading, but the text does not say so.

8. 6.2's grace and 6.4's forfeit are not related to each other; 6.4 simply cancels "late fees accrued", which is unproblematic only because grace suppresses fees rather than accrual.

adjudicator_reports.spec_defects:
None of the 30 cases turns on a genuine gap — every one is settled by an express rule (1.2/1.3 counting, 7.2's deemed same-date order, 4.2 voiding, 5.3/7.1 on the Override's ceiling, and 6.3's express statement that collection periods keep running). The defects below are real silences in the text that these cases happen to steer around, plus two places where the drafting invites a wrong-but-arguable reading.

1. Shelving on a closed day (4.3). The item is 'shelved on its return date', and 1.4 lets a return be credited to a closed day via the return box. The spec never says whether shelving (or the start of the collection period) moves to the next open day when the return date is closed, even though it does provide for the period's LAST day falling closed. T16/T17/T19 all have open shelving dates, so the gap is untested but live.

2. Lapse-and-reshelve on a closed day (4.3). 'The item is shelved the following day for the next member' has the same hole: if the following day is a Sunday, is that the shelving date, or does it move? In T17 18 March is open, so it does not matter.

3. 'Fewer than n days before' (1.2 / 2.3). 1.2 defines a period running FORWARD from D, and 2.3 asks a backward question about a registration date. The mapping works, but the text never states it directly; a drafter should have written 2.3 as 'checkout date is within 30 days after registration'. T05 has a 3-day margin, so no reading changes the answer.

4. Unnecessary Override invocations (5.1/5.2/5.4). 5.2 defines a 'valid invocation' only by reference to denials it cures. If a member invokes the Override on a request that no rule would deny, it is unclear whether the invocation is 'valid' (and so imposes the 7-day term of 5.4 in place of the class term, and burns the loan's one invocation under 5.1). Not squarely raised here — in T24, T27 and T28 the Override is genuinely needed.

5. Forfeit and 3.4 (6.4 vs 3.4). After forfeit the item is out, fees are cancelled, and nothing further accrues; the spec never says whether it remains 'OVERDUE' for the purposes of 3.4's 'any OTHER item overdue' bar or 3.6. Untested here (T25's vice is at 6 overdue days).

6. Same-type simultaneity (7.2). The deemed order sorts event TYPES but not two events of the same type on the same untimed date — e.g. two payments, or two returns. 4.1 supplies a tiebreak for same-date holds (member number), which highlights the absence of a general one.

7. Post-forfeit return and the hold queue (6.4 vs 4.3). If a forfeit item is later returned and a valid hold stands on it, 4.3's 'shelved on its return date' presumably still applies, but 6.4 is silent on the item's shelf status. Untested.

8. Distractor design worth flagging: T24's '23 March' and T28's '26 May' options are only reachable by counting the Override term from the request date, or by using the class term instead of 7 days. 5.4 forecloses both, so the options are wrong rather than arguable — but they show where a careless reader lands.

adjudicator_reports.spec_defects:
All 30 cases are, in my reading, decided by the text; the distractor options track identifiable misreadings (counting D itself, computing from the unmoved due date or the request date, ignoring the closed-day extension, double-counting cancelled fees). The defects below are real gaps in the specification, though none of them is load-bearing for these particular cases — which is itself worth noting: the suite exercises the well-specified core and leaves the soft edges untested.

1. Shelving on a closed day (4.3 vs 1.4/1.6). 1.4 credits a return-box deposit on a closed day to that date, and 4.3 says a held item is "shelved on its return date". So a collection period can start on a closed day, and nothing extends or delays its start — only its last day is protected. Untested here (all returns in the cases fall on open days), but the rule is silent.

2. 4.3's second and later collection periods. The extension "if its last day is closed it runs instead to the next open day" is attached grammatically to the first member's period; the successor's "fresh 4-day period counted from that day" does not restate it. Nor does the spec say whether "the item is shelved the following day" must be an open day. T17 escapes this only by luck (18 and 22 March are both open). A variant of T17 landing on a Sunday would be genuinely undecidable.

3. Consequence of a second Override invocation (5.1). 5.1 says a loan "carries at most one invocation, successful or not", but never says what a second invocation does: whether the accompanying renewal request is void, or simply judged as an ordinary request. T30 is insulated because 3.5 denies on independent grounds; a case with no hold and no other bar would be contestable.

4. Precedence list omits 2.2 and 4.2 (7.1). 2.3 is ranked but the 3-loan/1-Restricted cap in 2.2 is not, and the void-hold rule 4.2 is not placed either. 5.3 patches 2.2 for the Override specifically, but the general order is incomplete.

5. "Overdue" after forfeit (3.4/3.6 vs 6.4). Once an item is FORFEIT, fees stop and the status changes, but the spec never says whether it continues to count as an "OTHER item overdue" for 3.4 (or as overdue for 3.6 if the forfeited loan is the one being renewed). A member with a forfeited item outstanding is unadjudicable.

6. Holds on a forfeited item (4.3 vs 6.4). If an item with a valid hold queue is forfeited and never returned, nothing says what becomes of the queue, or what happens if it is returned after forfeit — is it shelved for the first holder, or does the hold survive at all?

7. Where the $75 replacement charge sits for suspension purposes. 6.5 posts it to the balance on the forfeit date, which will normally trigger 6.3 suspension, but 6.4 calls it a "replacement charge" rather than a late fee and 6.3 speaks of "unpaid balance"; the link is inferable but never stated.

8. 4.1 scope. "A hold may be placed on an item on loan" leaves unstated whether a hold may be placed on a hold-shelf item (4.5 says it is not a loan) or an open-shelf item — so an item that goes to the open shelf under 4.4 has no defined hold mechanics at all.

9. Calendar boundary. 1.3's "moves forward to the next open day" and all day-counting assume the March–May window; nothing defines behaviour for a computed date falling past 31 May (e.g. a 7-day Override renewal from a late-May due date).

author_self_flagged:
Ranked by how much a single clause is carrying the verdict, most fragile first. All 30 keys were re-derived mechanically (a Python model of Rules 1.1-1.3, 3.1-3.2, 4.3, 5.4, 6.1-6.4 reproduced every date, fee and window; 113/113 checks passed), so the residual risk below is interpretive, not arithmetic.

1. T15 (same-date payment cures suspension). The whole verdict rests on Rule 7.2's deemed ordering putting payments before renewal requests. A reader who treats 7.2 as a tie-break for genuinely conflicting events rather than a general sequencing rule could hold the balance at $24 and answer DENIED. 7.2's trigger ("the facts do not establish their order") is on its face general, and the probe says no times were recorded, but this is the probe most dependent on one clause being read broadly. If any probe should be dropped in a sensitivity check, this is it.

2. T19 (suspension does not pause the collection period). Textually explicit — 6.3's last sentence says collection periods keep running during suspension — but it cuts against a strong fairness intuition, since she was barred from collecting by the very same rule. Readers may resist the text rather than misread it, which shows up as disagreement even though the spec settles it.

3. T30 (second Override invocation). Turns on 5.1's "successful or not". A reader might distinguish an invocation that was *spent* on a granted renewal from one that failed, and read the loan as still having an invocation available. 5.1 covers both cases in terms, but the phrase is short and load-bearing.

4. T14 (hold placed later the same day). Relies on 7.3 ("each request is judged on the facts at its own moment") to establish that a hold logged at 15:10 does not unwind a grant made at 08:40. 7.3 says it, but it says it only once and in a section a reader may skim as boilerplate.

5. T17 (two-stage hold queue). No interpretive gap I can find — 4.1 confines the member-number tie-break to same-date holds and 4.3 spells out the re-shelving day and the fresh period — but it chains four computations (queue order, Sunday extension, lapse, fresh period), so it is the probe most likely to produce a wrong answer for reasons unrelated to what it is testing.

6. T09 (overdue day 29 vs forfeit at end of day 30). Robust in text but decided by a one-day margin across a month boundary; failures here will be miscounting rather than genuine indeterminacy, which makes it a noisy item even though it is well determined.

Two things I deliberately hardened rather than shipped as-is: Rule 1.3's final sentence ("All later computations... use the effective due date, never the unmoved date") was added because T10 is undecidable without it, and Rule 4.4 was reworded from "no valid hold remains" to "no valid hold stands on it" because T12's only hold was void from the outset and "remains" presupposes one existed. Rules 5.3 and 7.1 state the Override's scope limits twice over, deliberately, so that T25/T26/T29 do not depend on an unstated precedence.
